To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the theoretical maximum efficiency for converting sunlight to electricity in a terrestrial environment is 86%, that this is a factor of two higher than the maximum efficiency achieved by the most efficient existing technology, that this theoretical maximum efficiency can be achieved by using solar energy to drive a thermochemical cycle, and that this thermochemical cycle requires no more than a few hours of sunlight per day.

the theoretical maximum for energy from the Sun is 1.73 x 10-3 watts per square meter, and that the maximum is obtained by focusing direct sunlight with an array of mirrors that have a reflectivity of 100 percent.
the maximum theoretical energy that could be derived from direct and diffuse solar radiation is 1.36 × 1018 W.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the theoretical limits on the conversion of sunlight into useful energy.
the theoretical maximum of energy from direct and from diffuse sunlight, for various conversion schemes.
the theoretical limits of the efficiency of solar-energy conversion schemes, and with the practical limits of the efficiency with which these schemes may actually be implemented.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the directivity of sunlight is not a significant factor in biological energy conversion, although it may be a significant factor in some other solar energy conversion schemes.
directivity and spectral temperature are both used in photosynthesis, but the relative importance of each is unknown.
direct sunlight is not a prerequisite for photosynthesis, but is a desirable feature for plants with small leaves.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found that the directivity of sunlight is not a significant factor in the photosynthetic efficiency of natural vegetation, and that we are not aware of any biological system that makes use of the high temperature of sunlight.
, for the most part, the biological systems we know about use the high spectral temperature, but not the high directivity, of sunlight.
the maximum theoretical energy available from sunlight is about 2 × 1014 W, and that the maximum theoretical power available from sunlight is of order 10 W per square centimeter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the directivity of the Sun's flux is a significant resource for solar energy schemes.

there is an upper bound on the energy that can be extracted from sunlight by any scheme, and that this bound can be calculated in terms of the directivity and spectral temperature of the solar flux and the efficiency with which the scheme converts sunlight to useful energy.

there is a theoretical maximum for solar conversion efficiency, independent of any specific conversion scheme, and that this maximum depends on the spectral temperature of solar light and on the directivity of the incident radiation.
